Let [MATH: A] be an [MATH: m \times m] matrix. Recall that a nonzero vector [MATH: \mathbf{v}_1] is an eigenvector of [MATH: A] corresponding to the eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda] if

Content:
[MATH: A\mathbf{v}_1 = \lambda \mathbf{v}_1.]

Content:
We can write this equation as

Content:
[MATH: (A - \lambda I) \mathbf{v}_1 = \mathbf{0}.]

Content:
Therefore, the matrix [MATH: A-\lambda I] maps the vector [MATH: \mathbf{v}_1] to the zero vector [MATH: \mathbf{0}{:}]

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{v}_1 \xrightarrow{A- \lambda I} \mathbf{0}]

Content:
Now suppose that there exists a nonzero vector [MATH: \mathbf v_2] that is mapped to the zero vector in two steps by the matrix [MATH: A-\lambda I.] That is,

Content:
[MATH: (A-\lambda I)\mathbf v_2 = \mathbf v_1 \qquad \textrm{and}\qquad (A-\lambda I)\mathbf v_1 = \mathbf 0,]

Content:
where [MATH: \mathbf v_1] is an eigenvector of [MATH: A] corresponding to the eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda.]

Content:
We can represent this schematically as a chain of mappings, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{v}_2 \xrightarrow{A- \lambda I} \mathbf{v}_{1} \xrightarrow{A- \lambda I} \mathbf{0}]

Content:
We call [MATH: \mathbf v_2] a generalized eigenvector of rank [MATH: 2] because it is mapped to the zero vector in two steps.

Content:
By the same idea, an eigenvector of [MATH: A] is a generalized eigenvector of rank [MATH: 1] because it is mapped to the zero vector in one step.
